chapter: Joining Goodman and views on arranging
title: Dissatisfaction with writing for dance bands
summary: In the 1946 Metronome interview he complained about the constraints of dance tempos and block writing.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I recall, when I was at the Institute, they had a file that George Hoefer and Marshall Stearns collected on you over the years, and one of them was

an interview that you did with George Simon at the Metronome in '46, and this was right after you had been writing for Ray McKinley and I got a real sense of your being dissatisfied with having to write for "dance bands", having to keep a steady tempo, a steady meter.

Bill Finegan got the same thing. That's why Sauter-Finegan came out the way it did. You'd write a block, it was mainly for rhythm and not much else. You'd write a section this way, and the reason was it had a rhythmic touch to it. The way it was played made the difference. But you know, as you write, pretty soon you can't think of anything anymore, you're so limited.
